Read About Wadi Rum

A valley Bedouin tribes have crossed for thousands of years, that one British officer's memoir turned into a myth, and that Hollywood now uses whenever a script calls for Mars.

The valley Lawrence made famous

Wadi Rum's modern fame starts with a book. T. E. Lawrence — the British officer who fought alongside Arab tribes against the Ottomans during the 1917–18 Arab Revolt — passed through this valley repeatedly during the campaign, and his memoir "Seven Pillars of Wisdom" describes it in a sentence that still appears on nearly every brochure written about the place: "vast, echoing, and God-like." The rock formation near the village entrance was renamed after that book in the 1980s, and Lawrence's Spring and Lawrence's House — a ruined structure he is said to have used, though the historical record is thinner than the signage suggests — both carry his name today.

It's worth being honest about what that fame actually represents. Lawrence didn't discover Wadi Rum — the Bedouin tribes who guided him had been crossing it for centuries, and the Nabataeans before them for centuries more. What Lawrence did was write about it in English, for a Western readership, at a moment when the Arab Revolt was already being mythologized in Europe and America. The valley's Lawrence associations are real, but they are also the layer of history that happens to be legible to visitors who arrive already knowing his name. The deeper history takes more digging.

The Nabataeans, before the legend

Long before Lawrence, Wadi Rum sat on a spur of the trade network the Nabataeans built between Petra and the Red Sea — the same civilization that carved the Treasury into Petra's cliffs. The reserve's one standing Nabataean structure, a partly-excavated temple near the Rest House, was uncovered in 1933 and completed by French archaeologists in 1997; it's modest compared to Petra, but it confirms that this valley was a working stop on a caravan route, not empty wilderness that history happened to pass near.

The Nabataeans left more than architecture. Scattered across the reserve are thousands of inscriptions and petroglyphs — some Nabataean, many older, in the Thamudic script used by pre-Islamic Arabian tribes. The Alameleh panel in the reserve's north sector is one of the densest concentrations: camels, ibex, hunters and riders scratched into the sandstone's dark desert varnish, some of it more than two thousand years old and still legible without a guide's flashlight. Reading them requires no special access — they sit in the open, exactly where the people who made them left them.

Why the rock looks like that

The formations that make Wadi Rum look otherworldly are the product of a very specific geology. The valley floor is granite and basalt, some of the oldest exposed rock in the region, capped by much younger Cambrian and Ordovician sandstone laid down when this part of Arabia sat under a shallow sea. Wind and flash-flood erosion have spent millions of years cutting into that sandstone unevenly — the granite base doesn't erode the same way the sandstone above it does — which is why the towers rise as steep-sided monoliths rather than eroding into rounded hills the way softer rock formations do elsewhere. Jebel Rum, the massif that gives the valley its name, tops out around 1,750m and is Jordan's second-highest peak; Jebel Umm ad Dami, near the Saudi border, edges it out as the country's actual high point.

The same erosion that carved the valley's arches and canyons also exposed the desert varnish — a thin, dark mineral coating — that the valley's ancient inscriptions are scratched into. The rock recorded its own history twice: once geologically, once by the people who lived on it.

The Bedouin who still live here

Wadi Rum Village is home to the Zalabia Bedouin, and the neighboring desert is used by the Zawaideh tribe — the same families, largely, who guided Lawrence a century ago, now running the jeep tours, camel treks and Bedouin camps that make up most of the reserve's tourism economy. This isn't a preserved reenactment; it's a continuation. The zarb dinner served at camp — meat and vegetables slow-cooked underground in a sealed drum — is the same technique Bedouin cooks have used for generations, adapted now to feed tour groups instead of extended families. The sage tea poured at every stop, the tents, the guiding itself: all of it is a living trade, not a museum piece performed for visitors.

That said, the tourism economy has changed the valley considerably since Lawrence's time. Wadi Rum was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011, both for its natural beauty and for the archaeological record scratched into its rock, and the reserve now balances several hundred thousand annual visitors against the grazing and habitation rights of the Bedouin families who were here first. The permit system, the entry fee collected at the Visitor Center, and the requirement that visitors travel with a licensed local guide rather than self-driving into the interior are all part of managing that balance.

Mars, without the CGI

If Wadi Rum looks familiar even to visitors who've never seen a photo of it, that's because film crews keep using it to stand in for other planets. "Lawrence of Arabia" (1962) filmed here first, but the list since then is long: "Red Planet," "The Martian," "Rogue One: A Star Wars Story," and "Dune" all shot scenes in the valley, drawn by the same landscape Lawrence described — a place that looks less like anywhere else on Earth than almost anywhere else on Earth does. The 2015 film "The Martian" used Wadi Rum so extensively for its Mars exteriors that some tour operators now sell it as a selling point in its own right, which says something about how thoroughly the valley's real identity and its on-screen one have merged in the popular imagination.

What to carry with you

Wadi Rum rewards slowing down more than almost anywhere else on a fast itinerary. The jeep tours cover a lot of ground quickly, and that's the right way to see the valley's scale — but the stillness that made Lawrence reach for "God-like" only shows up when the engine stops: at the top of a dune at sunset, inside a canyon after the group ahead has moved on, under a night sky with no light pollution for fifty kilometers in any direction. The valley has been a trade route, a battlefield, a film set and a UNESCO site, and it carries all of that without contradiction, because none of it required changing the rock. Whatever else Wadi Rum has been asked to represent, it has mostly just had to sit there and be itself. That turns out to be enough.
